-   "notes": "THREE BUILDING FACTS ABOUT CHICAGO IN ONE PARAGRAPH, THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE.

1. THE SAUGANASH HAS JUST BEEN REFITTED — 'repaired, fitted up and furnished with neatness and taste'. The building is old news; its CONDITION on 1 July 1835 is not, and this says it was freshly done up and not shabby. 'so far as it goes' is the editor's qualification and it means small, not poor.

2. THE LAKE HOUSE IS UNDER CONSTRUCTION IN KINZIE'S ADDITION AND IS NOT YET FINISHED OR NAMED. 'There is a new house building in Kinzie's addition [to be] named we understand, the "Lake House."' Both halves matter: it is a BUILDING SITE at the scene date, north of the main branch, and even its name is reported at second hand ('we understand'). Anything the reconstruction puts on that spot on 1 July 1835 should be a structure going up, not a hotel open for business. This is the only dated statement of the Lake House's state that this corpus has produced.

3. NO HOUSE IN CHICAGO IS BIG ENOUGH, and the editor says where the big one should be: 'about double the size of that latter, erected this side of the river about the centre of Lake Street or in that vicinity.' That is a PROPOSAL and not a building — nothing stood there — but it fixes the Lake House's scale by comparison (a house double it would be the town's largest) and it tells you where the commercial centre of gravity was felt to be: the middle of Lake Street, south of the river.

WITH THE OTHER CLAIMS IN THIS READING RANGE the town's public houses at the scene date are: the Sauganash (refitted, unplaced here), the Exchange Coffee House (corner of Lake and Franklin), the Eagle Coffee House or Trowbridge's (Dearborn Street vicinity), the Tremont House (Dearborn Street), the New-York House (Lake Street), and the Lake House (building, Kinzie's Addition). Six houses and not one of them, on the editor's account, adequate.

The column is clipped at the right edge line by line; every supply is bracketed and none of them invents a name, a size or a street."

   "research_note": "LATER ADDRESS CHECK: Fergus's Directory of the City of Chicago, 1839, published in 1876, lists the Lake House at "Rush and North Water sts" in its Hotels section (p. 37). That line has been checked directly in the printed page image. Andreas instead names Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets. These later street accounts remain in disagreement: this reading does not locate or describe the building site on 1 July 1835. Its existing placement and reconstructed construction stage remain unchanged.

LATER COMPLETED-STATE PICTURE, NOT JULY 1835 CONSTRUCTION EVIDENCE: kellogg_blanchard_1856_old_fort_lake_house identifies the 1856 Kellogg/Blanchard print (the misleadingly named chicago_fort_dearborn_river_mouth_1830.jpg). Its labelled Lake House is the completed hotel right of the foreground fort blockhouse, partly behind a tree; the scene is approximately 1836–1849. The Images link is contextual and does not establish the height, roof or construction progress of this unfinished July 1835 shell. No camera, geometric match or grade promotion is claimed. A BUILDING SITE IS A STATE, AND THIS RECORD IS AN ARGUMENT ABOUT ONE. Everything about the finished Lake House is documented - brick, three storeys and a basement, nearly $100,000, five named backers, opened in the autumn of 1836 - and the scene-year press records an active project, but not its height, roof or detailed progress on 1 July 1835. THREE SOURCE PROBLEMS TRAVEL WITH IT AND ALL THREE ARE RECORDED ON THE ATTRIBUTES. (1) THE 1835 GROUNDBREAKING IS NOT ANDREAS. It comes from the uncredited editorial paragraph on chicagology_prefire112, which sits under a transcribed Andreas passage with no typographic break, drops Andreas's basement, and gives $90,000 where Andreas gives nearly $100,000. data/exclusions.json sources the same claim to drloih_hotels, a second unfootnoted compilation. That editorial groundbreaking date is not two independent witnesses, but the separate Chicago Democrat notice of 10 June 1835, page 2 column 5, already cited under function, does report a new house building in Kinzie's Addition, understood to be named Lake House. Its held transcription has bracketed supplies; no newspaper scan was newly inspected. The notice supports the project before the scene, not an exact groundbreaking date or progress, and the discrepancy in the cost is the proof that the paragraph is not restating the text above it. (2) THE STREET NAME IS A TRAP. Andreas twice puts the house at Kinzie, Rush and Michigan streets, fronting Michigan. North-side Michigan Street is today's East Hubbard Street, one block north of Kinzie; it is not Michigan Avenue, which did not cross the river until 1920. The gloss 'near where the Wrigley Building stands today' - on chicagology_prefire112 and repeated in docs/research/03-structures-north.md section 3.8, which also renders the street as 'Michigan (Water)' - moves the site about 150 m and across Kinzie Street, and appears to be a modern confusion of the street with the avenue. This record follows Andreas. (3) THE PROGRESS BY JULY IS THE INTERESTING GAP AND IT STAYS OPEN. The best anchor found is J. D. Bonnell's letter to the Chicago Times of 15 March 1876, quoted by Andreas, which describes walking the town the morning after arriving and seeing 'the Lake House in course of construction'. Bonnell dates that arrival to 25 August 1835 - eight weeks after the scene date - though the same letter's 'forty years ago' implies 1836 and Andreas's own lead-in says 1837. The 1837 reading is impossible on the letter's own content, since the hotel was open by the autumn of 1836. Harriet Martineau, in June 1836, still calls it 'a new hotel then building'. So the structure was demonstrably unfinished in mid-1836 and probably visibly rising in late August 1835, and this record retains one storey of roofless brickwork as a reconstructed worksite choice, with the honest range stated as zero to two storeys. Being unfinished in 1836 does not prove roof absence in July 1835. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: the Chicago American, whose first issue is 8 June 1835 and which would have reported a $100,000 hotel going up; the Chicago Democrat; or the Kinzie's Addition conveyances. See docs/RESEARCH/lake_house_construction.md.",

+## T-2379 — retain the editor's comparison without making it a measurement (2026-11-04)
+
+An editor requesting a hotel “about double” the Lake House's size expresses a desired
+relative size; it supplies no dimensions, existing-building ranking, July construction
+stage or vacant-site proof. The existing c001 interpretation and visitor Record now say
+so, retaining the exact quotation and earlier Fergus address ruling. No physical change
+is justified by this proposal. The original image-match ticket remains open and partial;
+further shell refinement requires dated construction evidence or an explicitly bounded
+reconstruction, rather than backdating the completed-hotel illustration into July 1835.
+

+## T-2379 — Lake House proposal distinguished from a measurement (2026-11-04)
+
+The visitor Record and admitted June 10, 1835 Chicago Democrat c001 interpretation now
+identify the suggested hotel “about double” the Lake House's size as an editorial
+proposal. It supplies no measured dimensions, existing-building ranking, July progress,
+or proof of a vacant proposed site. “Unfinished building” also replaces “unfinished frame”
+in the same note so the attestation does not imply an unsupported timber material.
+
+This is an interpretation correction, not a new newspaper reading or facsimile inspection.
+The quotation remains transcription-mediated; quote, normalized text, locator, reading,
+other claims and the merged PR1694 Fergus address ruling are exact. Phases, geometry,
+grades, resolved inputs and native MASTER/WEB files are unchanged. No new native or visual
+execution is claimed. Validation and the actual current hosted eight-part gate are recorded
+in the PR/evidence checkpoint. The July shell remains reconstructed and T-2379 OPEN/partial;
+the later completed-hotel picture does not establish July 1835 construction progress.
+
